631.title: The gurdwaras left behind
631.hook: a prayer for free access to Nankana Sahib and the gurdwaras across the border
631.howItsDone: Since Partition, the Ardas has asked for open access to Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras in Pakistan; Sikh pilgrims cross for major festivals, and the Kartarpur corridor has at times allowed day visits from India.

segments.voice: Yesterday: fateh, and your line: feed and protect. Did you feed someone, or stand beside them? Today, one of the newest lines in the Ardas, added within living memory. Day six hundred thirty-one.

On the Indian side of the border in Punjab, near the town of Dera Baba Nanak, there's a viewing platform. For years, people climbed it with binoculars to look across a few miles of fields at a white building on the other side. They couldn't go there. Many of them never would. They just looked, sometimes for a long time, and some of them wept. The building was Gurdwara Kartarpur Sahib, where Guru Nanak spent his last years and died. It's in Pakistan now. And every day, all over the world, the Ardas asks for a door to open. Today: the gurdwaras left behind.
screen: `A PLATFORM AND BINOCULARS.` → `A WHITE BUILDING ACROSS THE FIELDS.` → `KARTARPUR, IN PAKISTAN NOW.`

segments.voice: At Partition, when British India was divided into India and Pakistan, the new border ran straight through Punjab. The violence of that year fell on Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike; huge numbers were killed and uprooted on both sides. Sikh families who had lived in western Punjab for generations left everything and moved east. And they left behind places at the heart of Sikh history: Nankana Sahib, where Guru Nanak was born; Kartarpur, where he farmed and died; Panja Sahib at Hasan Abdal; Gurdwara Dera Sahib in Lahore, where Guru Arjan was martyred; and many more. After Partition, a new line entered the Ardas. In paraphrase: grant the Khalsa the gift of open access to see, serve and care for Sri Nankana Sahib and the other gurdwaras and holy places from which the Panth has been separated. The word for that separation is vichhora, the ache of being parted from someone you love. It's the same word Gurbani uses for the soul parted from God. Notice what the prayer asks for. Not ownership. Not conquest. Khulhe darshan deedaar: to see them freely. And sevaa sambhaal: to serve and look after them. For decades, Sikh pilgrims have crossed in groups for the great festivals, with permission from both governments. More recently, a corridor opened that let pilgrims from India walk to Kartarpur Sahib for the day, though whether it is open has depended on relations between the two countries. Some of the people on that viewing platform finally went. The prayer is still said, every day, for the rest.
screen: `PARTITION: A BORDER THROUGH PUNJAB.` · `NANKANA, KARTARPUR, PANJA SAHIB.` · `VICHHORA: THE ACHE OF BEING PARTED.` · `TO SEE AND SERVE, NOT TO OWN.` · then, large: `DOORS LEFT BEHIND.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look toward the west. If you can, turn to face west, toward the setting sun, the direction of Nankana Sahib from Indian Punjab. If not, just picture a horizon. Think of a place you can't go back to: a childhood home, a town, a country, a person's house. Let yourself feel the vichhora, the ache of it, without hurrying it away. Then think of the people for whom a door did open. If you pray, you can say Waheguru toward that horizon. The bell holds the time.
Vichhora, the ache of being parted from a place or person you love: the Ardas asks to see and serve freely the holy places across the border, Nankana Sahib and Kartarpur among them.
Your line: doors left behind. Call or message someone who's far from a place they love, and ask them to tell you about it. Day six hundred thirty-one.

632.title: Honor of the humble
632.hook: the Ardas names God by what God is to those with nothing: honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless
632.howItsDone: Near the end of the Ardas, Sikhs address God as nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, the honor, strength and shelter of those without them, just before the specific request of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday, vichhora, and your line: doors left behind. Did you ask someone far from home to tell you about a place they love? Today the Ardas turns from places to people, the ones nobody notices. Day six hundred thirty-two.

Every school has the kid who eats lunch alone. Every office has the person whose name nobody quite remembers. Every family has the cousin who is always in the kitchen while the photos are being taken. People often reach for big titles when they address God: king, judge, almighty. Near its end, the Ardas also does something quieter. Just before the one praying turns to their own request, the prayer names God by who God is for exactly those people. The kid at the empty table. The one in the kitchen.
screen: `THE KID WHO EATS ALONE.` → `BIG TITLES FOR GOD.` → `THE ARDAS CHOOSES QUIETER NAMES.`

segments.voice: The line runs like this, in Punjabi: nimaaniaan de maan, nitaaniaan de taan, niotiaan di ot, sache pita Waheguru. Honor of the dishonored, strength of the weak, shelter of the shelterless, true Father, Waheguru. Look at how the three names are built. Maan is honor, dignity, a sense of standing. Taan is strength. Ot is shelter, something to lean on. Put ni- in front of each and you get the people who lack it: the nimaana, with no standing; the nitaana, with no strength; the niota, with no one to lean on. So the Ardas doesn't describe God floating far above. It describes God as the thing each kind of empty person is missing. If you have no honor, God is your honor. If you have no strength, God is your strength. This isn't a new idea dropped into the prayer. Guru Nanak said it in his own hymns. In Sri Rag, on ang 15, he says Nanak stands with the lowest of the low, and has no wish to copy the great. And he adds that where the lowly are cared for, that is where the Lord's glance of grace falls. Sikh life tried to make that physical. In langar, everyone sits on the same floor and eats the same food, whatever their caste or their bank balance. In the Ardas the whole congregation, the rich donor and the person who came in for a free meal, says these words together, standing side by side. So the line works two ways at once. It is comfort for anyone who feels small today. And it is a quiet question for anyone who doesn't: if God's honor is with the overlooked, where should mine be?
screen: `MAAN, TAAN, OT: HONOR, STRENGTH, SHELTER.` · `NI-: THE ONES WHO LACK IT.` · `GURU NANAK STANDS WITH THE LOWLY.` · `LANGAR PUTS IT ON THE FLOOR.` · then, large: `STRENGTH OF THE WEAK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit comfortably and bring to mind one person who gets overlooked: at work, at school, in your building, maybe in your own family. See their face. Notice what they might be missing today: standing, strength, or someone to lean on. Don't fix anything yet. Just hold them in your attention, the way the Ardas holds them. If you pray, you can say the three words softly: maan, taan, ot. Then think of one small way to stand with them this week. The bell holds the time.
Maan, honor, dignity, standing: the Ardas names God as the honor of those with none, the strength of the weak, the shelter of the shelterless, maan, taan, ot.
Your line: strength of the weak. Today, stand with one overlooked person: sit with them, say their name, ask their opinion and actually listen. Day six hundred thirty-two.

633.title: The petition
633.hook: here the one praying says why this Ardas is being made
633.howItsDone: In the gurdwara, a family can ask the granthi to name their purpose in the Ardas, a birth, a journey, a remembrance; at home, the person praying names their own reason at the same point.

segments.voice: Yesterday, maan, and your line: strength of the weak. Who did you stand with? Today, right after naming God that way, the Ardas finally says what it's for. Day six hundred thirty-three.

Sunday at the gurdwara. The congregation stands, hands joined, and the person leading the Ardas has been speaking for several minutes: the Gurus, the martyrs, the Khalsa, the gurdwaras far away, the honor of the humble. Then the voice changes slightly. A name is spoken. A family's name, perhaps. A new baby. A grandfather's surgery next week. A shop opening on Main Street. A student leaving for college. For a few seconds, a prayer that belongs to a whole people becomes about one household's Tuesday.
screen: `THE CONGREGATION STANDS.` → `A FAMILY'S NAME IS SPOKEN.` → `ONE HOUSEHOLD'S TUESDAY.`

segments.voice: This is the petition, the part of the Ardas where the reason is named. Everything before it is fixed and shared. The opening invokes the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib. Then come the remembrances, the requests for the Khalsa and for the Sikhs, the line about maan. Then, at this point, the one leading says something like: in Your presence, this Ardas is made for, and the reason is named in plain words. The congregation listens and joins the waheguru that follows. Some readers trace the word ardas to a Persian word for a written petition, the kind a person would hand up to a ruler's court. Whatever the root, the picture fits. A petition is not a speech. It's short, it's specific, and it names what is being asked. And notice who can be named. Not only the person leading. A family can ask the granthi to include their purpose: thanks for a safe journey, a new job, the anniversary of a death, a child's exam. At home, a person praying alone names their own reason the same way. Nothing in the prayer asks for the reason to be grand. A petition only asks that it be plain. There's something steadying in that structure. The big, shared prayer holds a whole people's history. Then, inside it, your small reason is given a place, said out loud, in front of the Guru. Nobody is too small to have their reason named. And the prayer doesn't stop at one household: before it ends, it turns back out toward everyone.
screen: `THE FIXED PRAYER COMES FIRST.` · `THEN THE REASON IS NAMED.` · `ARDAS: A PETITION TO A COURT.` · `SHORT, HONEST, SPECIFIC.` · then, large: `SAY WHY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say your reason simply. Sit and let today's real concern rise. Not the one you think you should have. The one that's actually there. A worry, a hope, a thank-you. Now put it into one plain sentence. No flourishes. Just: this is for my mother's appointment. This is for the interview. This is thanks for the week. If you pray, you can say that sentence quietly to the One. If not, just let it sit in the open. The bell holds the time.
The petition. The moment in the Ardas when the reason for this prayer is named in plain words, inside a prayer that belongs to everyone.
Your line: say why. Today, when you ask someone for something, say the real reason in one honest sentence. Notice how it changes the asking. Day six hundred thirty-three.

634.title: Forgive our mistakes
634.hook: the Ardas asks forgiveness for any letter added or missed, any slip in the reading
634.howItsDone: After a reading or recitation, the Ardas includes akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni, asking forgiveness for any syllable added or missed and any error in the reading.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the petition, and your line: say why. Did one honest sentence change how you asked for something? Today, right after the reason is named, the Ardas does something humble. Day six hundred thirty-four.

A family has just heard the whole Guru Granth Sahib read aloud. That's an akhand paath: one unbroken reading, day and night, the readers taking turns while the house sleeps. At the end, the family stands for the Ardas. And somewhere in it comes a request that sounds almost like a proofreader's note. Forgive any letter added. Forgive any letter missed. Forgive every slip. After all that care, the readers still ask pardon for the mistakes.
screen: `ONE UNBROKEN READING.` → `READERS TAKING TURNS.` → `FORGIVE ANY LETTER MISSED.`

segments.voice: The Punjabi phrase is akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni. Akhar is a letter, a syllable. Vaadha is something added, ghaata something left out. Bhul is a mistake that comes from forgetting or not knowing. Chuk is a slip, a miss. Maaf karni: please forgive. It's said after a reading, a recitation, a kirtan, any time the words of the Guru have passed through human mouths. Why would a letter matter so much? Because for Sikhs the Guru Granth Sahib is not a book about the Guru. It is the Guru, the living teacher in words. Reading it is something like speaking in the Guru's own voice, and care with every syllable is a form of respect. But the line is not anxious. It doesn't promise that the reading was perfect. It assumes it wasn't. Guru Nanak said as much in Sri Rag, on ang 61: everyone makes mistakes; only the Guru and the Creator never do. That's not an insult to the readers. It's just the truth about people, said without drama. So the Ardas builds an apology into its own structure. The pattern is plain: the best care a reader can give, an admission that it probably fell short, then letting it go. A reader who had to be perfect might never open the book. A reader who knows the pardon is already part of the prayer can stand up, open it, and begin. And the request is made for everyone who read, so it covers every reader's slips, not one person's.
screen: `AKHAR: A LETTER, A SYLLABLE.` · `BHUL CHUK: FORGETTING, SLIPPING.` · `EVERYONE ERRS BUT THE GURU.` · `DO YOUR BEST, THEN ASK PARDON.` · then, large: `FORGIVE THE ERRORS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: apologize once. Sit and think back over the last day or two. Let one small slip come up: a sharp word, a forgotten text, a promise that slid. Don't pile on more. One is enough. Notice how it feels in your body. Then picture saying sorry to that person in a single plain sentence, no excuses attached. If you pray, you can ask the One to forgive the errors, yours and theirs. When the sit ends, send that apology, or plan when you will. The bell holds the time.
Bhul chuk, mistake and slip: the Ardas asks pardon for them, akhar vaadha ghaata bhul chuk maaf karni, any letter added or missed, any error at all.
Your line: forgive the errors. Today, make one apology without a but in it. And when someone else slips, let one go without comment. Day six hundred thirty-four.

635.title: The Ardas's last line
635.hook: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala: through the Name, rising spirits; by Your will, good for all
635.howItsDone: Every Ardas ends with Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala; the congregation then bows, and many follow with the couplet about the Guru Granth and the jaikara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, bhul chuk, and your line: forgive the errors. Did you make an apology with no but in it? Today we reach the very last words of the Ardas. Day six hundred thirty-five.

How do you end something big? A letter ends with love. A speech ends with thank you. A phone call ends, in some families, with five rounds of okay, bye, okay, bye. Last words carry weight because they're what stays in the room. The Ardas has walked through Sikh history, the Gurus, the martyrs, the homes left behind, today's specific reason, an apology for any slip. And then it ends on one line, the same line every single time, in gurdwaras from Amritsar to Toronto.
screen: `HOW DO YOU END SOMETHING BIG?` → `LAST WORDS STAY IN THE ROOM.` → `THE SAME LINE, EVERY TIME.`

segments.voice: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Take it in two halves. The first half: Nanak naam chardi kala. Naam is the Name, the Sikh word for living in awareness of the One. Chardi kala is rising spirit: a spirit that climbs instead of sinking, hopeful and steady even in hard times. Sikhs read the first half in more than one way. Some hear: Nanak, through the Name may there be rising spirits. Others hear: through the Name given by Nanak, rising spirits. Either way, the source of the uplift is the Name, not luck or mood. The second half: tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Tere bhaane, in Your will. Sarbat, everyone, all of it. Bhala, good, well-being. In Your will, may there be good for all. Notice what this does after everything that came before. Moments ago the prayer was about one family's surgery or one student's exam. Now it widens all the way out. Not good for Sikhs. Not good for the people in this room. Good for all, sarbat, with no one left off the list. And notice the order. Rising spirits first, then good for everyone. A sinking spirit has a hard time wishing anyone well. A climbing one can afford to be generous. This line is recited at the close of the Ardas, not found as a verse in the Guru Granth Sahib itself; it gathers up ideas that run all through it. When it's said, the congregation bows, and the prayer is done.
screen: `NAAM: THE NAME.` · `CHARDI KALA: A RISING SPIRIT.` · `TERE BHAANE: IN YOUR WILL.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA: GOOD FOR ALL.` · then, large: `RISING SPIRITS, GOOD FOR ALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a rehearsal for tonight. Sit tall. On an in-breath, think: chardi kala, rising spirit. Let your chest lift a little. On the out-breath, think: sarbat da bhala, good for all. Let the good go out past this room, to your street, your city, people you'll never meet, someone you find hard. Do that a few times. If you pray, you can say the whole line softly: Nanak naam chardi kala, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala. Tonight, before sleep, end the day with it. The bell holds the time.
Chardi kala, rising spirit, optimism that climbs even in hard times: through the Name, Nanak naam chardi kala; in Your will, good for all, tere bhaane sarbat da bhala.
Your line: rising spirits, good for all. Tonight, make it the last thing you think before sleep. If someone annoyed you today, include them. Day six hundred thirty-five.

636.title: The Guru is the Granth
636.hook: after the Ardas many recite the couplet: by the Timeless One's command the panth was founded, and all Sikhs are to accept the Granth as Guru
636.howItsDone: After the Ardas, many congregations recite the dohra aagiaa bhai akaal ki… guru maaniyo granth, then bow before the Guru Granth Sahib and raise the jaikara.

segments.voice: Yesterday, chardi kala, and your line: rising spirits, good for all. Did you end the day with it? Today, what many Sikhs say in the moment right after that line. Day six hundred thirty-six.

The Ardas is over. Everyone has bowed. In many gurdwaras, before anyone sits, a few more lines ring out, sung or chanted, often by the whole hall at once. They aren't a prayer, exactly. They're closer to a reminder, said aloud, of who is in charge here. And who is in charge is sitting right there at the front of the room, under a canopy, wrapped in cloth: a book. The scripture itself.
screen: `THE ARDAS IS OVER.` → `A FEW MORE LINES RING OUT.` → `WHO IS IN CHARGE HERE?`

segments.voice: The couplet goes, in its best-known form: aagiaa bhai akaal ki, tabhi chalaayo panth. By the command of the Timeless One, the panth, the Sikh community, was set on its way. Sabh sikhan ko hukam hai, guru maaniyo granth. All Sikhs are commanded: accept the Granth as Guru. It often continues: accept the Guru Granth as the visible body of the Gurus, and whoever wishes to meet the Lord, seek in the Shabad, the Word. Here's the history it remembers. In 1708, at Nanded in the Deccan, Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Guru, was near death. Sikh tradition says that instead of naming an eleventh human Guru, he placed the line of Gurus in the scripture, the Adi Granth, which from then on is called Guru Granth Sahib. Spiritual authority went to the Word; the community, the Khalsa panth, would carry it in the world. The couplet itself is not from the Guru Granth Sahib. It's a later verse from the Sikh tradition, and historians discuss exactly when it took this form. But the idea it states is the center of Sikh practice. That's why, in a gurdwara, the Granth sits higher than anyone. Why people bow before it. Why it's put to rest at night and opened again at dawn. The respect isn't for paper and ink. It's for the voice of the Gurus that Sikhs hear in those pages. So the line guru maaniyo granth isn't a slogan. It's an instruction about where to look: for Sikhs, to seek the Guru is to open the Word.
screen: `BY THE TIMELESS ONE'S COMMAND.` · `1708: GURU GOBIND SINGH AT NANDED.` · `THE LINE OF GURUS PASSES TO THE WORD.` · `SEEK THE LORD IN THE SHABAD.` · then, large: `GURU MANEYO GRANTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a bow. If you're in a gurdwara, you can bow before the Guru Granth Sahib the way the congregation does. If you're somewhere else, sit quietly and let your head lower a little, slowly, the way you'd nod to a teacher you respect. Notice what it feels like to bow to wisdom rather than to a person's power. Then rest there, breathing, as if you were waiting for a teacher to speak. If you pray, you can say Waheguru once as your head comes up. The bell holds the time.
Nanded, where in 1708 Guru Gobind Singh placed the Guru's authority in the scripture: Sikhs call it Guru Granth Sahib, and seek the Guru in its Word.
Your line: guru maneyo granth. Today, when a question comes up, go to a source you trust and read before you decide. Look to the word. Day six hundred thirty-six.

original.note: Gurmukhi: accept the Granth as the Guru; the line many recite after the Ardas.

trapdoor: what you thought: Sikhs treat a book as holy.
what it means: Sikhs treat the scripture as the living Guru, the voice of the ten Gurus in words.
what a scholar hears: the dohra is post-scriptural and its exact origin is debated, but it encodes the 1708 transfer of Guruship to the Granth and, with it, the role of the Khalsa panth.

637.title: The cry of joy
637.hook: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal: whoever says it is blessed, true is the Timeless
637.howItsDone: After the Ardas and at joyful or solemn moments, one person calls bole so nihaal and the congregation answers sat sri akaal; sat sri akaal is also an everyday Punjabi greeting.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nanded, and your line: guru maneyo granth. Where did you look for an answer? Today, the shout that often follows, and a look back at the week. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

If you've ever been near a gurdwara on a big day, or at a Sikh parade, you've heard it. One voice calls out: bole so nihaal! And a whole crowd answers, louder than seems possible: sat sri akaal! It can shake windows. It comes at the end of the Ardas, at weddings, at the start of a procession, sometimes from a single grandmother at the kitchen table when the news is good. It isn't a quiet prayer. It's a cry of joy, and it has a name: the jaikara.
screen: `ONE VOICE CALLS.` → `A WHOLE CROWD ANSWERS.` → `THE JAIKARA.`

segments.voice: Inside the word jaikara, some readers hear jai, victory or praise, the word in a cheer of triumph. It's a call and response. The first half, bole so nihaal: whoever says it will be nihaal. Nihaal is a lovely word: blessed, fulfilled, full to the brim with joy. The second half, sat sri akaal: true is the Timeless One. Sat is truth. Sri is a word of honor. Akaal is the one beyond time, the name Sikhs use for God who has no beginning and no death. Put it together: whoever says this is filled with joy, because the Timeless is true. Sikh tradition links the jaikara with Guru Gobind Singh and the Khalsa, and in Sikh history it was raised before battle, a way of reminding fighters that the outcome belonged to the Timeless. Today it's raised at every kind of moment. And the second half has a life of its own. Sat sri akaal is also an everyday greeting in Punjabi, hello and goodbye, with the truth of the Timeless folded inside. Now, the week we just finished. Day 631, vichhora, prayed for from across a border. Then maan: God as the strength of the weak. The petition, where the reason is named. Bhul chuk. The last line, rising spirits, good for all. The couplet, Nanded. And now the jaikara, the shout that closes it. A week that walked from grief, through humility and honesty, out into joy.
screen: `JAI: VICTORY, PRAISE.` · `NIHAAL: FILLED WITH JOY.` · `SAT SRI AKAAL: TRUE IS THE TIMELESS.` · `THIS WEEK: GRIEF, HUMILITY, JOY.` · then, large: `SAT SRI AKAAL.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say it once, clearly. Sit up. Take a full breath. If you're somewhere you can, say it out loud: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal. If you're on a bus, say it inside, but give it the same full voice in your head. Then sit with the echo. Notice what changed in your chest and shoulders. A jaikara isn't meant to be muttered. It's meant to lift. Stay with that lift, breathing, until the bell. The bell holds the time.
Jaikara. The Sikh cry of joy: bole so nihaal, sat sri akaal. Whoever says it is filled with joy; true is the Timeless One.
Your line: sat sri akaal. Today, greet one person with it, or with your warmest hello, and mean the truth inside the greeting. Day six hundred thirty-seven.

it was raised before battle in history; today it marks every kind of moment.
